Data-entry staff cannot merge individual ballots, and cannot clear a test score (only change it). More: staff-access.md , staff-invitations.md .

h: The working copy on this device
What syncs live and what needs an upload
What changes the cloud without your upload
x: Backups, restore and cloud sync  CrabbyTab is local-first: each device keeps a full working copy of the tournament, and the cloud copy in Firestore is shared between devices, private URLs and the public site. Some records sync live between administrator devices; the rest go up with Upload now . This page explains what is where, how to keep devices in step, how conflicts are handled, and how to back up and restore. Developer detail: storage-and-scale.md , live-collaboration.md , data-import-export.md . The working copy on this device  Each tournament's working copy is stored in the browser's IndexedDB (keys crabbytab_t_{slug}_… ). Older copies in localStorage are moved there automatically on first use. If IndexedDB is unavailable (some private-browsing modes), localStorage is used with its ~5 MB limit. Draws, allocations, standings and breaks are computed in the browser from this copy, so the tab room keeps working offline. If the browser cannot save (for example the disk quota is full), the app shows Could not save … locally and retries with the next change. The working copy belongs to one browser profile on one device. Clearing site data deletes it. A second tab on the same device sees the other tab's changes after a reload. A tournament that has never been uploaded is local only : nothing leaves the device, and its public pages work only on that device. What syncs live and what needs an upload  For a tournament with a cloud copy, an administrator's device is live (status pill Live ) while it is online and live updates are not paused: Data How it reaches the cloud and other admin devices Ballots, debates (draw, allocation, per-side results), teams and adjudicators (check-ins, availability, details) Live , record by record, within seconds. Offline changes are queued and sent on reconnect. Tournament settings, rounds (including releases), motions, rooms, break categories, feedback, institutions, audit log Upload now (other devices get them with Download and compare or a reload) Things to know: Only debates and ballots of the active round are listened to. A correction to an earlier round reaches other devices when they reload or download. A release changes the round , so releases upload and publish in one step (see below). Another device sees a new draw's debates live, but the round's status only after the upload reaches it. Data-entry assistants are not live: they use their own Upload (see below). To work without live writes on one device, open the cloud status menu → Pause live updates on this device ( Resume live updates turns them back on). While paused, every change waits for Upload now . The page warns before you close it while changes are not uploaded or live writes are still queued. Opening a cloud tournament merges the cloud copy into this device's copy using the same rules as a download. The cloud status menu  The status pill in the top bar opens the Cloud sync menu. The pill shows one of: Live , Connecting… , Uploaded , N changes not uploaded , Offline , Offline — N queued , Local copy , Syncing… , N sync conflicts , N upload conflicts , Upload incomplete , N double confirmations , Live updates stopped or Sync failed . The menu explains the state, lists pending changes per collection and shows the last result. Its actions: Action What it does Upload now Sends this device's changes to the cloud and publishes public pages. Download and compare Merges the cloud copy into this device. Resolve sync conflicts (N)… Opens the conflicts dialog (only when there are conflicts). Pause / Resume live updates Per device and tournament (administrators). Export archived cloud versions Downloads the recovery file (shown after conflicts). Administrators also have Upload and Download buttons next to the pill. Signed-out users see Sign in to upload . Both ask for confirmation first. Upload now  Queued live writes are flushed first (up to 20 seconds), so the checks below see them. Only records changed since this device last synced are sent, in batches. For each record: Situation Result New in the cloud Written at version 1. Same content Nothing written. Cloud unchanged since this device last had it Your version is written at the next version; the replaced cloud version is archived. Cloud changed by someone else since then The cloud version is kept. Yours is archived as a conflict. Deleted on this device Soft-deleted in the cloud ( deletedAt ); the previous cloud version is archived as recoverable. Already deleted in the cloud Not resurrected; yours is archived. Audit events Append-only: only events the cloud does not have are added. If nothing conflicted, the public pages are republished. If any record conflicted, public pages are not updated (the message says so): download, choose versions, and upload again. Due automatic emails (draw and results notifications) are sent; see Email and notifications . Other rules: an upload never changes the owner or administrators of a cloud tournament, and is refused if the cloud tournament belongs to someone else and you are not one of its administrators. The first upload reserves the tournament's URL; a URL already taken is refused. If an upload stops part-way, everything committed so far is kept, the pill shows Upload incomplete , and public pages are not updated. Upload again to finish; every write is safe to repeat. This also completes a regenerated draw whose cloud write was interrupted. Download and compare  Merges the cloud copy into this device, record by record: records not changed here since the last sync take the cloud version; records changed here are kept, and become sync conflicts if the cloud changed them too; records only in the cloud are added; records deleted in the cloud, or deleted here and not yet uploaded, are dropped; no cloud records are deleted. Resolving conflicts  Resolve sync conflicts (N)… (cloud status menu or account menu) opens the Sync conflicts dialog. It lists each record changed both here and in the cloud, with a table of the fields that differ ( This device / Cloud ). For each record choose Keep mine or Use cloud , or use Keep all of mine / Use all cloud versions (both ask for confirmation). This device's version stays in use until you choose. Versions you keep go up with the next upload, which archives the cloud version it replaces. Double confirmations : if two devices confirm different ballots for the same debate before seeing each other's, the pill shows N double confirmations . Nothing is resolved automatically; open the debate's ballots and discard the version that should not count. Live updates stopped means the cloud refused a live write (for example the account lost its admin role). Those records count as not uploaded and show as conflicts once the cloud version arrives; nothing is silently dropped. The recovery file  Every replaced or conflicting cloud version is archived in the tournament's syncConflicts collection (append-only). Account menu → Export sync recovery (administrators, online) downloads all of them as {slug}-sync-recovery.json ( crabbytab-sync-recovery-v1 ). There is no screen for browsing archived versions; restore anything you need by re-entering it or editing a backup. What changes the cloud without your upload  Live writes from other administrator devices. Ballots, feedback and self check-ins from private URLs and public forms. Uploads by data-entry assistants. API writes. Each bumps the record's syncVersion , so a stale upload from another device becomes a conflict instead of overwriting it. Data-entry assistants have a single Upload button that sends only the participant, ballot, feedback and result changes they are allowed to make, through a server-checked route. Settings, draws and allocations are never uploaded from their device. See Staff and roles . Publishing public pages  Public pages and private URLs read a published snapshot of the cloud copy, not live data (see Public pages and releases ). Upload now publishes automatically when it had no conflicts. Releases (draw, results, motions, tabs, breaks, participant lists) upload and publish as one action. They are refused while offline or while records conflict with the cloud. Saved on this device only. After saving settings that public pages or private URLs read (tournament settings, public forms, staff access), a notice says the change is on this device only and offers Upload and publish . After it succeeds: "Uploaded and published. Public pages and private URLs now use this setting." Account menu → Republish public pages rebuilds the snapshot from the cloud copy . If this device has changes not uploaded, it asks first ( Upload and publish , or Publish cloud copy anyway ). After an incomplete upload or conflicts it is blocked until you Upload again or Download and compare . Backups  Account menu (administrators): Export tournament backup → {slug}-backup.json ( crabbytab-tournament-backup-v1 ): every collection, full fidelity. This is the recovery format. Export DebateXML archive → {slug}-archive.xml : the Tabbycat-compatible exchange format. It never contains emails, private URLs, passcodes or feedback comments, and may omit fields DebateXML cannot represent. Export a backup before each round and before risky operations (regenerating a draw with results, deleting rounds, restoring, changing format). Restore tournament backup…  Account menu → Restore tournament backup… and choose the file (valid JSON, at most 50 MB). The file is checked before anything changes: format version, the tournament record, required fields, duplicate ids, records from another tournament, and references (missing rounds, teams, debates, adjudicators or break categories are errors; missing venues, motions and institutions are warnings). You see, per collection, how many records are only in the backup, only on this device, different or the same. Choose: Merge : add the backup's missing records; records on this device win. Replace : make the tournament match the backup, after an explicit confirmation. A {slug}-pre-restore-backup.json of the current data downloads first. The tournament's id, URL, owner and administrators are kept, the audit log is merged (never replaced), records not in the backup are queued as cloud deletions, and a backup.replaced audit event is recorded. A restore changes this device only. Upload now afterwards to update the cloud copy. Recommended routine  Keep live updates on for every administrator device; check the pill says Live . After setup changes, use Upload and publish (or Upload now ) so other devices and the public site get them. Other devices Download and compare before editing settings, rounds, motions, rooms, breaks or feedback. Export a tournament backup at the end of each round. If an upload reports conflicts, export the sync recovery file before doing anything else, then resolve them. Details  Firestore is the source of truth for the live collections; the remaining collections move to live sync in later steps of the sync model adopted in the parity plan . Live writes are field-level patches committed in one atomic batch per command, so two devices changing different fields (or different rounds' availability) of the same record do not overwrite each other. An adjudicator panel is one unit: last write wins. Tab-room rules (locked ballots, completed rounds, double entry) are checked on the device before a live write; the server checks only the Firestore security rules. If the browser cannot keep the Firestore offline cache (some private-browsing modes), queued offline writes are lost when the tab closes. Large events: the first upload of a 1000-team tournament is about 10,000 writes, within the free plan's 20,000 a day, but several full uploads a day are not; plan on the Blaze plan for events of that size.

API and tokens  CrabbyTab has a REST API (v1) for one tournament at a time. It mirrors Tabbycat's v1 API (v2.12.1): reads of almost everything the tab room holds, and writes that run through the same commands, rules and audit log as the tab room. Use it to drive a projector display, a bot, a results feed or your own tooling. This page is a summary. The full reference is docs/api.md . Every deployment also serves a generated reference page at /tournaments/api and an OpenAPI 3.1 document at /api/openapi.json . Both are generated from the same route definitions the server enforces. Creating a token  Open the account menu (top right) → API access ( /{slug}/api ). Only tournament administrators see it. Under Create token , give the token a name (for example "Projector display"). Choose the Access : Public : what the public site shows ( read:public ). It cannot be combined with other scopes. Administrator : for each area, choose None , Read or Read and write . The scopes are listed under the table before you create the token. Press Create API token . The token ( ct_live_… ) is shown once . Copy it then; only a SHA-256 hash is stored. Active tokens lists each token with when it was created and last used. Revoke deletes it at once. Tokens belong to one tournament. Treat them like passwords: keep them out of browser code, source control and URLs. Scopes  Scope Grants read:public Exactly the published, release-gated public view. read:<area> Administrator read access to one area, unreleased data included. write:<area> Read and write access to one area. Area Covers tournament Tournament, preferences, feedback questions, score scales and criteria, speaker categories, schedule events rounds Rounds and motions participants Institutions, teams, speakers, adjudicators venues Venues and venue categories breaks Break categories, eligibility and breaks draws Pairings, draw generation, adjudicator allocation, preformed panels results Ballots feedback Adjudicator feedback checkins Availability and check-ins standings Team, speaker, reply and adjudicator standings (read only) staff Staff permission groups (read only) No scope ever returns private URL keys, passcodes or email addresses. Staff access cannot be granted through a token: only a signed-in administrator can do that on the Staff page (see Staff and roles ). Tokens created before per-area scopes ( read:public , read:draws ) keep working. Public reads without a token  Every endpoint a read:public token may use also answers requests with no Authorization header , as Tabbycat's anonymous access does. Both see the same published public view: draws once released, panels once revealed, motions and results once released; team, speaker and reply standings, and the participant and institution lists, only once released (403 before); public tab limits apply as on the public page. These reads come from the cached public snapshot, so they cost no Firestore reads. API writes, like tab-room changes, reach public reads only when the tournament is published (see Backups, restore and cloud sync ). Anonymous requests are limited to 60 per client address per minute; use a read:public token for more. Participant keys ( /me )  A participant can use the key and passcode from their private URL slip instead of a token: curl -H "Authorization: Key team_abcd2345efgh" -H "X-Passcode: k3j9m2xx" \ https://HOST/api/v1/tournaments/SLUG/me The key can be a team's, an adjudicator's or a speaker's own private URL key (see Private URLs and portals ). With it a participant can do what their portal does, under the portal's own rules: Endpoint What it does GET /me Who the key belongs to (a speaker's key identifies their team, with speakerId ). GET /me/ballots , POST /me/ballots See the ballots the portal shows; a voting adjudicator submits a ballot (refused when private-URL ballots are off). GET /me/feedback , POST /me/feedback See and submit feedback along the tournament's feedback paths. PUT /me/checkin Self check-in for the current round, when self check-in is on. Unknown keys and wrong passcodes get the same 401. Attempts are limited to 120 per client address per hour. Ballot receipts are not emailed for API submissions. Main endpoints  All paths are below /api/v1/tournaments/{slug} . Rounds are addressed by sequence number ( /rounds/3 ), everything else by id. Area Read Write Tournament / , /preferences , /feedback-questions , /score-criteria , /schedule-events , /speaker-categories PATCH , PATCH /preferences , POST /publish Rounds /rounds , /motions create, update (release draw, reveal panels, release results, complete), delete Participants /institutions , /teams , /speakers , /adjudicators create, update, delete Venues /venues , /venue-categories create, update, delete Draws /rounds/{seq}/pairings , /rounds/{seq}/preformed-panels generate-draw , allocate-adjudicators , hand-made pairings, pairing edits, preformed panels Results /rounds/{seq}/ballots , /rounds/{seq}/pairings/{id}/ballots submit, confirm, discard, unconfirm Breaks /break-categories[/{id}/eligibility or /break] categories, eligibility, generate or clear a break Check-ins /rounds/{seq}/availabilities , …/checkin availability, check in or out Feedback /feedback submit, confirm, ignore, delete Standings /teams/standings , /speakers/standings , /speakers/standings/replies , /adjudicators/standings — Standings take ?round=N (standings after round N), ?category= (a break or speaker category) and ?metrics=a,b,c (rank by those metrics for this request). Metrics with no data yet are null , never 0, as in Tabbycat. Large lists are paginated with limit (1–200, default 50) and cursor , and return { "data": [...], "nextCursor" } . How writes behave  Same rules as the tab room. A write runs a tab-room command in one Firestore transaction; a refused write changes nothing. A rule violation is 409 rule_violation with violations[] . If every violation is overridable, repeat the request with "override": { "reason": "..." } ; the reason is recorded in the audit log. Hard rules cannot be overridden. Versions. Each changed record gets the next syncVersion and the replaced version is archived. Send expectedVersion on a PATCH to get 409 conflict instead of overwriting a concurrent change. Deletions are soft. Regenerating a draw. POST /rounds/{seq}/pairings/generate-draw on a round that already has a draw is refused with 409 conflict unless you send "replaceExistingDraw": true , as in Tabbycat. Earlier versions always regenerated; clients that relied on that must add the flag. Double entry. With double entry on (see Ballots and results ), a token counts as one person: it cannot confirm a ballot it entered without an override. A blind check ( checksVersion: N ) that differs from version N is refused with 409 conflict and a differences[] list; confirm version N instead, or resend with "acceptDifferences": true . Ballots are sent as the ballot form records them; points, wins, margins and voting majorities are computed by the server, never accepted from the client. Audit. Each write is recorded with actorId: "api-token:<id>" , the token name and the request id. See Audit log . Other devices. Ballots, debates, teams and adjudicators reach open admin devices live; other changes arrive on their next download. Unknown query parameters and body fields are rejected with 422, so typos are never ignored. Limits and errors  Limit Value Requests per token 300 per minute (per server instance) Requests per client address 600 per minute (per server instance) Anonymous requests 60 per client address per minute (per server instance) Writes per token 1000 per hour (shared across instances) /me attempts 120 per client address per hour (shared across instances) Writes per request 450 Firestore writes, else 413 Errors are { "error": { "code", "message", ... } } with codes bad_request (400), unauthenticated (401), forbidden (403), not_found (404), method_not_allowed (405), conflict / rule_violation (409), payload_too_large (413), validation_failed (422), rate_limited (429, with Retry-After ) and internal (500). On the free Spark plan, standings and availability reads load the tournament's teams, debates and ballots; use them sparingly. Public and anonymous reads cost nothing. Differences from Tabbycat  Not mapped: site-wide users and global institutions, web-push registration, Tabbycat's generic /questions , and listing, creating or deleting tournaments (a token belongs to one tournament). Staff and group membership cannot be written through a token. Anonymous ballot and feedback creation is through the public forms, not the API. Speakers check in with their team; a debate's check-in is its paper-ballot receipt. A pairing's importance uses CrabbyTab's 0–10 scale, so Tabbycat's negative levels are refused. Ids are strings; standings use CrabbyTab's configured precedence. Serializers do not yet carry team references, pronouns or last names. Details  Implementation: src/lib/api/v1/ (route definitions in routes/ , dispatch in http.ts , writes in session.ts and tabRoom.ts ); every endpoint is served by src/app/api/v1/[[...path]]/route.ts . GET /draws is the first v1 endpoint, kept with its original response shape for existing clients. Every response has Cache-Control: no-store and an X-Request-Id header. A token's "last used" time is written at most once an hour.

Audit log  CrabbyTab records significant tab-room actions as audit events : time, who did it, category, action, a summary, and details captured at the time. What is recorded  Categories: tournament , draw , allocation , ballot , standings , break , feedback , venue . Examples: Area Actions Draws draw.generated (with the random seed and requested options), draw.status_changed (confirm, release), draw.debates_updated , draw.deleted Allocation adjudicators.allocated (with remaining clashes), manual assignments, preformed panels; venue.assigned (room allocation) Results ballot.submitted , ballot.confirmed , ballot.discarded , ballot.received , ballots.resaved (after a scoring change) Feedback feedback.submitted , feedback.reviewed , feedback.deleted Breaks break.generated , break.cleared , break.categories_updated , elimination.round_advanced Setup rounds, motions, venues, teams, adjudicators, institutions created/updated/deleted; entities.batch_saved (CSV import); tournament.settings_updated ; private_urls.regenerated Other rules.overridden (with the reason, before the overridden action runs), backup.replaced , rehearsal.results_simulated / rehearsal.feedback_simulated (with the seed) Round releases (results, motions) appear as round.updated with the changed fields. Writes through the API are recorded too, attributed to the API token ( api-token:<id> ) or the participant key. Not recorded: email sends, data-entry staff confirmations (stored on the ballot instead) and private-portal submissions outside the API. No IP addresses are stored. Viewing  Admin → Audit log ( /{slug}/audit , tournament administrators) lists events newest first, with actor, category, action, round/debate ids and an Event details disclosure. Events are stored with the tournament and uploaded with it (see Backups, restore and cloud sync ). In the cloud they are append-only : the Firestore rules forbid editing or deleting them, and a user event must name its real author. Restoring a backup merges the log rather than replacing it. Publishing a verifiable log  Upload the tournament first: the release reads the cloud copy. On the Audit log page, Release audit log (later: Update public snapshot ). The card shows when it was last released and how many events; events newer than the snapshot are marked. View public log opens /{slug}/audit/public . What is published: sequence number, timestamp, category, action, summary and hashes. Never actors or details. The events are hash-chained at release time: ordered by time, each hash is SHA-256 of crabbytab-audit-v1 , the previous hash and the event's public fields, starting from 64 zeros. The public page downloads the snapshot and verifies the chain in the visitor's browser , so anyone can check that the published history is consistent. Up to 5,000 events per release. Limitations  The chain proves the released snapshot is internally consistent. It cannot prove that nothing was left out before release, and each release rebuilds the chain from the current cloud log. Anyone with Firebase console or service-account access can change stored events outside the rules. The tab room keeps the whole log in the browser (it is not paged). More: tournament-rules-enforcement.md , api.md .

Choosing a language For yourself Staff pages: open the account menu (top right of the navbar). The Language section lists every language plus Automatic . Public pages, portals, public registration, the home page, the tournament list and the setup wizard: use the language button in the page header. (The sign-in page has no button; it uses your saved choice or browser language.) It shows the current language's own name (for example "Deutsch"), so a reader who cannot read the current language can still find it. Your choice is saved in this browser only ( localStorage ), not in your account. It does not follow you to another device. Choose Automatic to clear it. For your tournament's participants Participants often leave their browser in English even when the tournament runs in another language. To set a default for them: In the sidebar, go to Admin → Configuration → Public visibility . Set Public pages and portals language . "Each viewer's browser language" (the default) means no tournament language. Save tournament settings. It does not apply to staff pages, which always use each staff member's own choice. It also does not apply to public registration ( /register/{slug} ), which uses the viewer's own choice or browser language. What is translated Translated: Public pages, public forms and public registration. Team and adjudicator portals, including check-in, feedback and ballot entry. Almost all staff pages: draw, allocation, results, standings, breaks, feedback, motions, settings, imports and exports, backups, staff access, email setup, private URLs, schedule and the projector. Short side codes (OG, OO, CG, CO, AFF, NEG) stay as codes in every language. Gotchas Offline: a language you have never opened before cannot load while offline. The page stays in English until you are back online. A language you have opened once keeps working offline. First moment of a page load: the page renders in English and switches as soon as the language loads. Most pages show a loading state at that time, so this is rarely visible. Machine-drafted wording: treat unusual debate terms as a translation issue, not a rule difference. Report them (see below). Reviewing a translation If you are fluent in one of the languages, a review is the most useful contribution you can make. Find the catalogue: src/lib/i18n/messages/locales/.json (Bengali is split across src/lib/i18n/messages/bn.ts and the src/lib/i18n/messages/areas/bn-* files). Each key's English text is in src/lib/i18n/messages/en.ts and src/lib/i18n/messages/areas/ . Switch CrabbyTab to the language and walk through the public tab, both portals and the pages you use most. Look for wrong debate terms, unnatural wording, and text too long for buttons or table headers. Edit the values only. Keep the following exactly as in English: {placeholders} such as {round} or {count} , … markup such as this portal , plural keys ( _one , _few , _many , _other , …) — the language needs every category it has, product names (CrabbyTab, Tabbycat, CSV, API). Run npm run i18n:check (see below). After the whole file has been reviewed, remove machineDrafted: true from that language's entry in LOCALES ( src/lib/i18n/config.ts ) in the same pull request. The "machine-drafted" labels then disappear. For Bengali, also remove the machine-drafted warning comment at the top of bn.ts . Partial reviews are welcome too; leave the flag on and say what you covered in the pull request. See Contributing . Details for contributors How it works CrabbyTab uses a small in-house typed dictionary in src/lib/i18n/ rather than an i18n library. Translated pages are client components; a client-side provider ( I18nProvider ) chooses the language with resolveLocale in src/lib/i18n/config.ts . English is bundled with every page and is the fallback: a missing key in any catalogue shows the English text. Other catalogues are lazy-loaded. Each is its own code-split chunk, fetched the first time that language is chosen and cached by the service worker afterwards. See loadCatalogue in src/lib/i18n/messages/index.ts and Architecture . Keys are type-checked. t("some.key") with a key not in the English catalogue fails the build. Plurals use Intl.PluralRules ; numbers, dates and lists use the Intl formatters from useI18n() . Each language has an intlLocale tag (for example ar-u-nu-latn keeps Latin digits). Adding a language Create the catalogue from the English source: npm run i18n:new -- sw This writes src/lib/i18n/messages/locales/sw.json with every English key (English text as the value to translate) and every plural category the language needs, worked out with Intl.PluralRules (extra categories start from the English _other text). The code must be a BCP 47 tag ( sw , pt-BR ). It refuses to overwrite an existing file unless I18N_OVERWRITE=1 is set. It then prints the remaining steps. Translate the values, following the rules in Reviewing a translation . Add an entry to LOCALES in src/lib/i18n/config.ts : { code: "sw", nativeName: "Kiswahili", englishName: "Swahili", intlLocale: "sw", machineDrafted: true }, Leave machineDrafted: true until a fluent speaker has reviewed it. Use an intlLocale such as xx-u-nu-latn if the language's default digits are not Latin. Right-to-left is detected from the code; nothing else to set. Add a loader line in src/lib/i18n/messages/index.ts (a literal import() path, so the catalogue becomes its own chunk): sw: () => import("@/lib/i18n/messages/locales/sw.json").then(json), Run npm run i18n:check . Check the public tab, both portals and a few staff pages in the new language, including the right-to-left layout if it applies. The language then appears in the language menu and the tournament public-language setting, and is matched against browser preferences. Checking catalogues npm run i18n:check runs the i18n tests ( vitest run src/lib/i18n ). It checks every catalogue, not just one; a language code after it is ignored. It reports: missing and unknown keys, missing plural categories for the language, {placeholder} and markup that differs from English, locale matching, text direction and the pre-paint script ( config.test.ts ), lookup, fallback, plurals and formatting ( translate.test.ts ). The same tests run in npm test , so a pull request that adds an English string must add the key to every catalogue (copy the English text if you cannot translate it, and say so in the pull request). See Testing . The two scripts live in tools/i18n/ ( run.mjs , template.ts , newLanguage.test.ts ). Adding a new string Add the key to the English catalogue for that area ( src/lib/i18n/messages/areas/… or en.ts ), use it with t() , plural() or rich() from useI18n() , and add it to every other catalogue. Never translate strings that are saved into records or compared in code. Full rules: docs/internationalization.md . For right-to-left support in new components, use logical Tailwind utilities ( ms-* / me-* , ps-* / pe-* , start-* / end-* , text-start / text-end ), gap-* instead of space-x-* , and rtl:-scale-x-100 on directional icons.

It saves only the settings you changed on the page. Settings you did not touch stay as stored, and a default shown in the form is never written just because you saved. Saving is refused, with a message, when: substantive speakers is not a whole number of at least 1; a speaker, reply (when reply speeches are on) or feedback (when feedback is on) minimum is not below its maximum, or one is empty; the speaker score step is not above 0; the minimum adjudicator score to vote is empty; the Rényi order or BP position cost exponent is below 0 or empty; a custom feedback question or a score criterion is invalid. Every save (from these pages, other pages or the REST API's PATCH /preferences ) is also checked against src/lib/setup/preferenceValidation.ts : each preference must have the right type, and an option must be one of its listed values. Ranges are given in the tables below. Locks once ballots exist. After the first ballot is entered, the format, teams per room, substantive speakers, reply speeches, ballot mode (preliminary), "Ballots ask for speaker scores" and score criteria cannot change, because existing ballots would no longer fit. The elimination ballot mode locks once the first elimination ballot is entered. Scoring changes after ballots. Changing score ranges, ghosts, margins, low-point wins, forfeits, bye results, winner declaration, aggregation, speech ranks, maximum margin, reply step or the reply-speaker rule after ballots exist raises a warning (a soft rule). Where team totals are affected, every entered ballot's totals are recalculated. See Ballots and results . Saved here, live after upload. Saving changes your working copy. Public pages, private URLs and other devices only see the change after you upload to the cloud. After saving, a notice offers to upload and publish. See Public pages and releases . Glossary  Terms as CrabbyTab uses them in its pages and code. Most follow Tabbycat's meaning; where CrabbyTab differs, the entry says so. UI labels are in bold . Adjudication core — the chief adjudicators. An adjudicator flagged Adjudication core is always a tester, can be listed publicly, and staff can be given the Adjudication Core permission group. See Participants and imports and Staff and roles . Adjudicator score — the strength used to allocate adjudicators: the test score (or base score when there is none) blended with the weighted feedback average by the round's feedback weight. See Feedback . AIDA rules — break rules of the Australasian Intervarsity Debating Association that limit how many teams per institution break (1996, 2016 Australs and 2016 Easters variants). See Breaks and eliminations . Assistant — Tabbycat's name for tab-room helpers without full access. In CrabbyTab they are data-entry staff , managed on Admin → Assistants (page Tournament access ). See Staff and roles . Availability — whether a team, adjudicator or room takes part in a round. Anyone without an availability record counts as available (Tabbycat counts nobody until checked in). See Check-ins and availability . Ballot / ballot version — a recorded result for one debate. Each save is a new version; the one confirmed, non-discarded version counts. See Ballots and results . Ballot intake — the Results → Ballot intake board that tracks printed ballot sheets by barcode: Missing , Received , Entered , Awaiting check , Confirmed or Disputed . See Printing and display . Base score — an adjudicator's rating before feedback ( Base rating (1–10) in the adjudicator dialog). Changes are kept in the score history. Compare test score . See Feedback . BP (British Parliamentary) — four teams per room in the positions Opening Government (OG), Opening Opposition (OO), Closing Government (CG) and Closing Opposition (CO). Teams earn 3, 2, 1 or 0 points by rank. See Tournament setup and formats . Bracket — in a power-paired round, the teams on the same score of the first team-standings metric (wins in two-team formats, points in BP). See Rounds and draws . Break — the teams that qualify for the elimination rounds of a break category, followed by its reserves. Generated on Results → Break . See Breaks and eliminations . Break category — an independent break, such as Open, ESL or Novice, with its own size, reserves, priority and rule. A general category includes every team not marked ineligible. See Breaks and eliminations . Bubble-up-bubble-down — an odd-bracket method that forms intermediate brackets and swaps a team with a neighbour when the pairing would clash. See Rounds and draws . Bye — a team sits out a round because the field does not fill every room. Bye team results decides whether it counts as absent or as a full win; it never gives speaker scores. In a partial elimination, a top seed's bye means it advances without debating. See Rounds and draws . Chair — the adjudicator who leads a panel. Chairs and voting panellists can submit ballots from their private URL. See Adjudicator allocation . Check-in — marking a team, speaker, adjudicator or room present, by tick, barcode scan or self check-in. With Check-in expiry , old check-ins stop counting. See Check-ins and availability . Cloud copy — the tournament stored in Firestore, shared by devices, private URLs, staff and the public site. Compare working copy . See Backups, restore and cloud sync . Code name — a team's public alias. With a code-name mode on, public pages show code names only and real names never leave the server; the Code names page decodes them for the tab room. See Public pages and releases . Composite team — a team whose speakers come from more than one institution. See Participants and imports . Conflict — a reason an adjudicator must not judge a team or sit with another adjudicator: personal, institutional, or a team–institution conflict. Allocation avoids them through a large penalty and lists any that remain. Conflicts are never public. See Adjudicator allocation . Consensus ballot — one result for the whole panel. Compare voting ballot . See Ballots and results . Data-entry staff — signed-in staff whose permission groups decide what they can do (enter ballots, check people in, and so on). Tabbycat's assistants. See Staff and roles . DebateXML — the XML archive format Tabbycat uses. CrabbyTab imports it as a new tournament and exports it. See Participants and imports . Double entry — a second person checks every tab-room ballot before it counts, by Review or by Blind re-entry. See Ballots and results . Draw — the pairing of teams into rooms and positions for a round. See Rounds and draws . Draw check — the list of errors and warnings for a draw (clashes, missing rooms, side imbalance and so on). Releasing a draw with errors needs a recorded reason. See Rounds and draws . Draw stage — where a round's draw is in its release: No draw , Draft , Confirmed, not released , Released to teams only and Released to public . The stored values are none , draft , locked , teams_released and confirmed ( released is read as a synonym). See Rounds and draws . Draw strength — a standings metric: the sum of a team's opponents' team points. Variants use opponents' wins, speaks or rank. See Standings and metrics . Equity — a permission group for equity officers: see and edit conflicts. It cannot see participant contact details. See Staff and roles . Feedback — ratings and answers about adjudicators from teams and other adjudicators, submitted on private URLs, public forms or entered by the tab room. See Feedback . Feedback path — who may give feedback on whom (for example chair on panellists, teams on the chair). See Feedback . Feedback weight — set per round on the Allocation page: how much the feedback average replaces an adjudicator's test or base score (0 to 1; new rounds default to 1). See Feedback . Fold / slide / adjacent — pairing methods within a bracket of ten: fold 1 v 10, slide 1 v 6, adjacent 1 v 2. See Rounds and draws . Forfeit — a two-team ballot option: the other team wins with 1 point, without speaker scores. See Ballots and results . Ghost speech — see iron-person speech . Global administrator — a site-wide administrator whose UID is in the server variable FIREBASE_ADMIN_UIDS . Only global administrators create tournaments. See Staff and roles . Importance — a debate's priority for allocation, 0–10, set by hand or by Prioritise by bracket / Prioritise by liveness . Preformed panels also have an importance. See Adjudicator allocation . Independent — a team or adjudicator with no institution ( Independent / unaffiliated ), so no institutional conflict applies. See Participants and imports . Info slide — background text released before a round's motions. Motion release has three steps: Not released , Info slides , Motions . See Public pages and releases . Intermediate bracket — a bracket formed between two brackets to absorb an odd team: the bottom team of the higher bracket meets the top team of the lower one. See Rounds and draws . Iron-person speech — a speaker giving an extra speech when their team is short. The extra speech is marked Ghost on the ballot: it never counts in the speaker tab, and counts towards the team score only with Team score includes ghosts . See Ballots and results . Live — the sync status of an administrator device whose ballots, debates, teams and adjudicators sync with the cloud copy record by record. See Backups, restore and cloud sync . Liveness — per break category, whether a team is live , safe (certain to break) or dead (cannot break), from the completed rounds. Shown in standings, on the Draw and Allocation pages. See Adjudicator allocation . Local only — a tournament that has never been uploaded: nothing leaves the device. See Backups, restore and cloud sync . Motion veto — a team striking one of the round's motions. With Record motion vetoes , ballots record one veto per team; vetoes feed the motion statistics. See Ballots and results . N teams per room — the format for rooms of any team count other than 2 or 4 (Tabbycat's teams in debate , used by its Public Speaking preset with 6). Positions are Team 1 … Team N ; only random and manual draws. See Rounds and draws . One-up-one-down — a conflict-avoidance method that swaps opponents between adjacent rooms to remove clashes. See Rounds and draws . Panellist — an adjudicator on a panel other than the chair. Panellists vote on voting ballots and may submit their own sheet. See Adjudicator allocation . Partial elimination — a first elimination round when the break size is not a full bracket: the top seeds get byes and the rest debate. See Breaks and eliminations . Passcode — the secret that goes with a private URL. It is separate from the link and can be printed on slips. See Private URLs and portals . Permission group — a named set of permissions given to data-entry staff, such as Tabulation assistant, Equity, Adjudication Core or a custom group. See Staff and roles . Postponed debate — a debate marked as not yet held; it gets no room and its result can come later. See Ballots and results . Power pairing — drawing teams against others on similar results: two-team rounds pair within brackets; BP rounds use Tabbycat's Hungarian assignment. Round 1 is drawn randomly. See Rounds and draws . Precedence — the ordered list of metrics that ranks teams or speakers (for example points, then total speaks). See Standings and metrics . Preallocated sides — two-team sides set on the Draw page before the draw. See Rounds and draws . Preformed panel — a panel built before the draw and placed as a unit by its importance. See Adjudicator allocation . Private URL — a participant's secret link ( /{slug}/private/team/… , /adjudicator/… or /speaker/… ), used with a passcode, that opens their portal: their draw, ballots, feedback and self check-in. No account is needed. See Private URLs and portals . Public form — an optional ballot or feedback form on the public site for participants without private URLs, with an optional password. Its submissions are always unconfirmed. See Public pages and releases . Public snapshot — the cleaned-up copy of released data that the server builds from the cloud copy when you publish. Public pages read only this. See Public pages and releases . Pull-up — a team moved up from a lower bracket to fill an odd bracket. Pull-ups are recorded on the debate and counted by the Pull-ups metric. See Rounds and draws . Release — making something visible to participants or the public: a draw stage, a round's results, team speaks, motions, or an item on the Public release panel. Releases upload and publish in one step. See Public pages and releases . Republish — Republish public pages (account menu) rebuilds the public snapshot from the cloud copy. See Public pages and releases . Reserve — a team listed after the breaking teams of a category (R1, R2, …); the Reserve size sets how many. See Breaks and eliminations . Room constraints — hard requirements a room must meet (category, seats, accessible, online, near tab room) and soft room preferences for room categories with a priority (Tabbycat's venue constraints). See Venues and constraints . Rules preset — a bundle of Tabbycat's settings for a named format (BP, Australs, WSDC, APDA, Public Speaking and others), applied when the tournament is created, or later to an existing tournament after a preview of every change. See Tournament setup and formats . Self check-in — a participant checking themselves in from their private URL. See Check-ins and availability . Self-split ballot — in a two-team voting round with one voting adjudicator, the adjudicator declares a 2:1 split. See Ballots and results . Side names — what the two sides are called: Affirmative/Negative (default), Government/Opposition, Proposition/Opposition, Pro/Con, Appellant/Respondent, Team 1/Team 2 or Plaintiff/Defense. BP uses OG, OO, CG, CO. See Tournament setup and formats . Silent round — a round whose results are kept off public results and standings. See Public pages and releases . Slug — the short name in a tournament's address, for example my-open-2026 . It cannot be changed later. Speaker category — a group of speakers such as ESL or Novice, managed on Setup → Speaker categories . Public categories get their own speaker tab; categories can also decide break eligibility. See Standings and metrics and Breaks and eliminations . Swing team — a team made up on the day to fill the last room instead of giving byes. It is drawn like any team, but it and its speakers are left out of standings and the break. See Rounds and draws . Test score — an adjudicator score from a test that, when set, replaces the base score in allocation. See Feedback . Tester — an adjudicator flag (always on for the adjudication core); the feedback pages note when a tester sat on an adjudicator's panel. See Participants and imports . Tournament administrator — a person with full control of one tournament (Tabbycat's tab director). See Staff and roles . Trainee — an adjudicator who sits on a panel without voting and cannot submit ballots. Only adjudicators marked as trainees can fill trainee slots. See Adjudicator allocation . Two-team formats — UADC (Asian), Australs, WSDC and custom two-team. See Tournament setup and formats . Upload now / Download and compare — the manual cloud sync for data that does not sync live (settings, rounds, motions, rooms, break categories, feedback and so on). Download compares the cloud copy with this device and shows conflicts. See Backups, restore and cloud sync . Voting ballot — one scoresheet per voting adjudicator; the majority decides. BP ballots are always consensus. See Ballots and results . Who-beat-whom — a standings metric that ranks two tied teams by their result against each other. See Standings and metrics . Working copy — the tournament stored in this browser (IndexedDB), where the tab room's edits happen and draws, standings and breaks are computed. See Backups, restore and cloud sync .

Comparison with Tabbycat  Tabbycat is the established open-source tab system. CrabbyTab is an independent project, not affiliated with Tabbycat. It follows Tabbycat's rules, algorithms and terms closely, but runs on free serverless hosting and does its computation in the browser. This page compares CrabbyTab on the current beta branch with Tabbycat v2.12.1 . The full record, including every audited row, is in docs/tabbycat-parity-plan.md . How the comparison was made  Source audits. Tabbycat v2.12.1's preferences, routes, REST API, models, management commands and algorithms were extracted from its source and checked one by one against CrabbyTab's code. This was done twice. The second audit was run by agents that had not written the fixes, had to cite code paths, and, for algorithms, ran Tabbycat's own Python against CrabbyTab on hand-made cases. It found about 60 bugs, which were fixed with regression tests. The rows are in docs/parity-audit/ (first audit) and docs/parity-audit/second-pass/ (second audit). Statuses there are recorded before the fixes. Differential tests. The same tournaments are run through real Tabbycat and through CrabbyTab, and the outputs are compared ( below ). Architecture  Tabbycat CrabbyTab Hosting Django + PostgreSQL server (Heroku, Docker, etc.) Next.js on Vercel + Firebase (free tiers) Where computation runs Server Browser: draws, allocation, standings and breaks (draws and allocation in a Web Worker) Tab-room data One shared database A working copy in each browser. Ballots, debates, teams and adjudicators sync live between administrator devices; everything else goes up with Upload now . See Backups, restore and cloud sync . Offline Needs the server The tab room keeps working offline; live changes are queued and sent on reconnect Public site Rendered from the live database A public snapshot built when you publish, cached on the CDN. See Public pages and releases . What matches Tabbycat  Unless a difference is listed in the next section, these follow Tabbycat's behaviour and option names. Formats and presets. BP, UADC, Australs, WSDC, custom two-team, and N teams per room (Tabbycat's teams_in_debate other than 2 or 4). All eleven Tabbycat rules presets: Australs, BP, Canadian Parliamentary, Australian Easters, NZ Easters, Joynt Scroll, UADC, WSDC, APDA, Karl Popper and Public Speaking. Side names (Aff/Neg, Gov/Opp, Prop/Opp and others). See Tournament setup and formats . N teams per room. The same scope as Tabbycat: random and manual draws, poly ballots (ranked on totals, advancing teams, or scores-only voting ballots), byes; power-paired, seeded, round-robin and generated elimination draws are refused, as in Tabbycat. See Rounds and draws . Draws. Two-team power pairing (odd-bracket methods, pull-up restriction, fold/slide/adjacent/random pairing, one-up-one-down, minimum-cost and minimum-cost-with-pull-ups), Tabbycat's Hungarian BP draw with its position costs and pull-up distribution, random, seeded and manual draws, Berger round robin by seed (two-team) and Tabbycat's BP round-robin tables, preallocated sides, sides chosen on the ballot, byes, swing teams, elimination draws with partial eliminations, and the draw stages draft → confirmed → released to teams → released . See Rounds and draws . Adjudicators. A differential test harness against Tabbycat itself (next section). Differential test harness  tools/tabbycat-diff runs the same tournaments through Tabbycat v2.12.1 and through CrabbyTab's own libraries and compares the outputs by rule. Fixtures (generated from a seed by fixtures/generate.ts , stored as DebateXML plus a config.json ): Fixture Covers bp-uneven BP, 26 teams with byes, Open/ESL/EFL break categories with priorities, iron-person speeches, adjudicator conflicts australs-voting Australs rules, uneven institutions, 3-judge voting panels with split decisions, replies twoteam-odd-ties Two-team, 19 teams (a bye every round), ranked on wins only (many ties, including at the break), side cap What is compared. For each fixture CrabbyTab imports the archive, applies Tabbycat's effective preferences, and computes standings after every round, a draw for every round (eight seeds), the break for every category and an adjudicator allocation: Standings and breaks value by value: every metric both engines compute, ranks, and breaking/reserve sets. Draws and allocations by the properties the rules constrain, because several answers can be valid: coverage, brackets, pull-ups, side imbalance, institution clashes, repeat pairings, side-cap violations, BP position cost and byes; for allocation, chairs present, hard conflicts, panel sizes and history repeats. The allocation is compared against CrabbyTab's ports of Tabbycat's Hungarian allocators, not CrabbyTab's own default strategy. Every discrepancy must be classified in known-differences.json as a rule difference, a CrabbyTab defect, a configuration difference or a valid alternative. A difference counts as a valid alternative only when CrabbyTab is no worse than Tabbycat on average and in its worst seed. The latest report shows all standings checks agreeing (2800/2800, 2496/2496, 2644/2644), no CrabbyTab defect and no configuration difference; the remaining rule differences are the tie-order and break-cutoff differences above. Running it. Tabbycat's output is committed as golden files, so the comparison needs no Docker or Python and runs as part of npm test : npx vitest run tools/tabbycat-diff  compare against the golden files TABBYCAT_DIFF_WRITE=1 npx vitest run tools/tabbycat-diff  regenerate the report after reviewing a change The test fails when a discrepancy has no verdict, or when the set of discrepancies differs from the committed report. Regenerating the golden files needs Tabbycat itself, through Docker or a native script with Python 3.11 and PostgreSQL; see the harness README . Limits: one Tabbycat version; elimination rounds, feedback, motions and venues are not compared; debate importance is 0 on both sides. See also Testing . How quickly the public sees a change
x: Caching, indexing and performance  How CrabbyTab keeps public pages fast and inside the Firestore free tier (Spark: 50,000 document reads per day), how search engines see a tournament, and what is known about very large (1000-team) events. For organisers  Public pages show the last published copy  Public pages, the projector ( /{slug}/display ) and private-URL portals never read your device. They read a public snapshot that the server builds from the cloud copy when you publish. Releasing something publishes it. Releasing or unreleasing a draw, results, team speaks, a motion, a tab, a break or a participant list uploads this device's pending changes and publishes public pages in one step. If the upload or the publish fails, the dialog says the change is saved on this device but not public yet . Upload now also publishes after the upload, unless the upload left sync conflicts (publishing then would mix your changes with older versions). Resolve the conflicts first. Republish public pages (in the top-bar menu, with Tournament settings and the backup actions) publishes again without other changes, for example after changing a public-visibility setting. Changes made only by data-entry staff reach public pages after the next administrator upload or publish. A tournament that has never been published is built live from its cloud collections and cached for five minutes. That is expensive for large events, so publish once before you share links. How quickly the public sees a change  Who is looking When they see the new version Someone opening or reloading a public page Within about 15 seconds (the CDN cache of the main response) A public page or projector left open At the next version check, every 45 seconds while the tab is visible Check-in status page Within about 15 seconds of the next publish Schedule page / calendar feed Within about 2 / 5 minutes Public pages open with the latest round straight away and load earlier rounds after it, so standings and results can fill in a moment later on big tournaments. Search engines  Admin → Configuration → Public visibility → Public homepage → Search engines (Tabbycat's search_engine_indexing ) has three choices: Choice Effect Allow every public page to be indexed (default) Public pages are indexable; the sitemap lists the public tab plus the schedule and check-in pages when they are switched on. Only the public tab homepage Only /{slug}/public is indexable; every other public page gets noindex, nofollow . The sitemap lists the public tab only. No pages Every public page gets noindex, nofollow ; the tournament is left out of the sitemap. Gotchas: noindex is a request; well-behaved search engines follow it, others may not. It is not a privacy control — anyone with the link can still open a public page. Hide information with the public visibility settings instead. The setting takes effect when you publish (it is read from the public snapshot). The cross-tournament motion statistics page ( /tournaments/motions/public ) is noindex whenever any tournament pooled there has a setting other than "all". Link previews (title, description, image when a link is pasted into chat apps) are produced whatever the setting. The description is the first paragraph of your public homepage (as plain text), else your welcome message, shortened to 160 characters, or a generated sentence. The tab room, projector, private URLs, sign-in, invitation and account pages are always noindex . Details  What costs Firestore reads  Activity Reads A visitor opening a public page Normally none: served from the CDN or the Vercel Data Cache. A cache miss costs one read per snapshot chunk it needs. Version checks from open public pages None after the first per publish (cached). A publish A few aggregation reads to check whether anything changed (skipped publish ≈ 3 reads + one per source collection); otherwise one full read of every public collection ( feedback only when a public feature needs it) plus writes of the changed sections. An administrator device opening a cloud tournament One read of every collection, then live listeners: about 325 reads for a 100-team BP event, plus about one read per change per other administrator device. A private-URL portal load Only that participant's debates, their teams and their ballots (about 10 debates for a team at a 1000-team BP event), via the participantIds index. Sitemap At most one read per published tournament every six hours. Pooled motion statistics About one read per contributing tournament per hour. Anonymous visitors never open Firestore listeners; only administrator devices do (see live-collaboration.md ). Publish-time snapshots ( src/lib/publicView/* )  projection.ts decides what is public (an allowlist: hidden values never reach a snapshot, a cache or a browser). derived.ts computes tabs and aggregates at publish time. See Security model . snapshot.ts splits the view into sections : base sections ( tournament , rounds , teams , adjudicators , venues , motions , breakCategories , institutions , checkins , tabs , derived ) and one round-{roundId} section per public round with that round's debates and ballots. Each section is hashed ( hash.ts ) and chunked into documents of at most about 700 KB. store.ts ( publishPublicView , called by POST /api/tournaments/[id]/public-view ): Skips the rebuild when the device's public fingerprint and the cloud source token (aggregation counts and syncVersion sums) both match the last publish. Otherwise reads the source collections, writes only the sections whose hash changed to publicViews/{slug}/chunks/{section}-{hash}-{i} , then switches the root publicViews/{slug} over in one write, then deletes chunks the new root no longer uses. Retires views published under an older slug and calls revalidateTag(publicViewTag(slug)) (tag public-view:{slug} ). The root also stores a small seo summary and, when motion statistics are released, a motionSummary , so the sitemap and pooled motion page never read whole snapshots. Vercel Data Cache  Server reads go through unstable_cache (Next.js 15; "use cache" is not used): Entry Key Revalidate Invalidated by Public view root public-view-root , slug 1 hour tag public-view:{slug} on every publish Section slug, section, hash, chunk count 24 hours never needed: content-addressed by hash Never-published fallback public-view-live , slug 5 minutes tag public-view:{slug} on first publish Sitemap sources public-sitemap-sources 6 hours tag public-sitemap (publishes deliberately do not clear it) Pooled motion summaries public-motion-summaries 1 hour none Because sections are cached separately and keyed by hash, publishing one round's results invalidates only the root and the sections that actually changed; every entry stays well below the cache's 2 MB limit. CDN headers  publicCacheHeaders(sMaxAge, staleWhileRevalidate) sends Cache-Control: public, max-age=0, s-maxage=…, stale-while-revalidate=… : browsers always revalidate, the CDN absorbs refresh storms. Route ( /api/public/... ) s-maxage / stale-while-revalidate tournaments/[slug] (base + latest round) 15 s / 30 s tournaments/[slug]?round={id}&h={hash} with the current hash 1 day / 1 hour (a content address) same with a stale or missing hash 15 s / 30 s tournaments/[slug]/version 10 s / 20 s tournaments/[slug]/checkins , /forms 15 s / 30 s tournaments/[slug]/registration 30 s / 60 s (60 s / 120 s when closed) tournaments/[slug]/audit (release status) 60 s / 300 s tournaments/[slug]/schedule 120 s / 600 s tournaments/[slug]/schedule/ical 300 s / 900 s motions (pooled statistics) 600 s / 3600 s Version polling and per-round paging  Public pages and the projector poll /version every 45 s ( PUBLIC_VIEW_POLL_MILLISECONDS ), only while the browser tab is visible, and refetch the projection only when the version changed. The main response holds every base section, the latest public round, and roundSections (round id → hash). Public pages then load the other rounds three at a time; the projector loads only the round it shows; private portals load every round first ( fetchCompletePublicProjection ). Rounds whose hash did not change are kept. Views published before per-round sections are still served (split by round when read) until the next publish rewrites them. robots.txt, sitemap.xml and metadata  src/app/robots.ts returns buildRobotsRules(resolveSiteUrl()) from src/lib/seo/robotsRules.ts : one rule for every crawler that allows / and the public pages ( /*/public , /*/public/… , /*/schedule/public , /*/checkins/public , /*/audit/public ) and disallows /api/ (including /api/public/ ), /login , /invite , /account , /forgot-password , /tournaments/new|import|demo , private URLs ( /*/private/ ), the projector ( /*/display ) and every tab-room section from TOURNAMENT_STAFF_SECTIONS . Because crawlers apply the longest matching rule, each disallowed section has a longer Allow for its public twin. It points to {site}/sitemap.xml . A test fails if a route folder under src/app/[tournamentSlug]/ is missing from the section list. src/app/sitemap.ts is rendered per request ( force-dynamic , so a build without credentials does not bake in an empty sitemap). It lists the site home page plus publicSitemapEntries for every published tournament ( publicViews/{slug} roots, at most 15,000): nothing under "none", the public tab (priority 0.8) under "homepage only", and under "all" also the schedule (0.5) and check-in (0.3) pages when switched on, with lastModified from the publish time. Without Firebase admin credentials or on a Firestore error it lists only the home page. Record pages, the audit log and the registration form are not listed but stay crawlable through links. Metadata. src/app/[tournamentSlug]/layout.tsx sets noindex, nofollow for everything under a tournament. Public pages override it in generateMetadata via publicPageMetadata ( src/lib/publicView/robots.ts ), which reads only the cached tournament section and returns a title ( {page} · {tournament} | CrabbyTab ), description, canonical URL, Open Graph and Twitter cards with /og-image.png , and robots from robotsForPublicPage . This covers the public tab (the "homepage"), team and adjudicator record pages, the public ballot and feedback forms ( /public/ballots , /public/feedback ), the schedule, check-in and audit pages, and the registration form. An unknown tournament is noindex ; any other read error keeps the page indexable so a transient failure does not drop it from search results. Absolute URLs use NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL , else https://$VERCEL_URL , else http://localhost:3000 ( src/lib/seo/site.ts ). Set NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL in production so the sitemap and canonical URLs use your real domain. Large tournaments (1000 teams)  From storage-and-scale.md : Device storage. The working copy is in IndexedDB (a 1000-team working copy is 7–13 MB, beyond localStorage's ~5 MB). Without IndexedDB (some private-browsing modes) it falls back to localStorage and its limit. Uploads send only records changed since the last sync, in transactions of up to 150 records. An initial upload of a 1000-team BP event is about 10,000 reads and 10,300 writes; uploading again with nothing changed is about 4 reads. Spark allows 20,000 writes a day, so plan on the Blaze plan for events of this size. Public snapshot after 9 rounds: about 5 MB (BP) or 8.4 MB (WSDC) in 18 sections, the largest under 900 KB; the first public response is 0.9–1.3 MB. Speed. Draws take up to about 3 s a round, standings under 0.1 s; auto-allocation is the slowest step (seconds per round) and runs in a Web Worker so the page stays usable. Large rounds can be split into shards on the allocation board. The benchmark ( src/features/tournament/application/scale.test.ts ) plays 2 rounds by default; CRABBYTAB_SCALE=full plays all 9 and CRABBYTAB_SCALE=off skips it. See Testing . Known limits  Publishing reads every public collection once (unless nothing changed), so publish when something is ready rather than continuously on very large events. Never-published tournaments are built live and may be too large to cache. A second browser tab sees another tab's changes to the same tournament only after a reload. Architecture  CrabbyTab is a Next.js 15 (App Router) + React 19 + TypeScript application with Tailwind CSS, Firebase Authentication and Cloud Firestore, deployed on Vercel. This page is for contributors. Read AGENTS.md for the engineering rules. Principles  Local-first. Draws, allocation, standings, breaks and validation are pure TypeScript functions that run in the organiser's browser. No paid compute service is involved. Deterministic and testable. Randomness goes through one seeded source ( src/lib/draw/rng.ts ). Domain logic is unit-tested without Firebase. Least privilege. Browsers talk to Firestore directly only as tournament administrators (plus two narrow direct writes for data-entry staff). Participants, most staff work, the public site and integrations go through server routes that use the Firebase Admin SDK. See Security model . Cheap reads. The public site is served from a snapshot built at publish time and cached, never from live collections (Spark tier: 50k reads/day). See Caching, indexing and performance . How data moves  Organiser device Firestore Vercel server ------------------- --------- ------------- IndexedDB working copy --upload/download--> tournaments/{id}/... <--Admin SDK-- /api/** routes TournamentContext <==live listeners==> (ballots, debates, | (pure libs compute) teams, adjudicators) v publicViews/{slug} (snapshot) | Public pages / portals <---------------- cached JSON from /api/public/** ---------+ 1. The working copy (IndexedDB)  Each tournament's working copy lives on the device in IndexedDB (database crabbytab , store kv ), under keys crabbytab_t_{slug}_{suffix} ( meta , rounds , teams , debates , ballots , feedback , auditEvents , syncBaseline , ...), each a JSON string. src/lib/offline/localStore.ts is the only code that touches it. TournamentContext loads one tournament's keys into memory when it opens, reads and writes synchronously, and flushes coalesced writes to IndexedDB in one transaction a moment later. A failed flush (quota, blocked storage) shows an alert and is retried with the next change. Older working copies in localStorage are migrated to IndexedDB on first use. If IndexedDB is unavailable the same store falls back to localStorage (about 5 MB). Theme, language and remembered portal passcodes stay in localStorage. public/sw.js is a service worker that caches the app shell and static chunks, so the app reopens offline. src/lib/offline/chunkRecovery.ts reloads once when a deploy has removed a chunk the page asks for. Draw generation and auto-allocation can run in a Web Worker ( src/features/tournament/compute/ ), so large draws do not freeze the page and can be cancelled. A tournament that has never been uploaded is local-only: nothing leaves the device. 2. Cloud sync (upload / download)  For collections that are not live (settings, rounds, motions, venues, break categories, feedback, institutions, audit events), the organiser syncs explicitly with Upload and Download and compare ( src/features/tournament/application/cloudSync.ts , infrastructure/tournamentRepository.ts ). Every cloud record has a syncVersion . The device keeps a sync baseline (version and content hash of each record at its last sync) and uploads only records changed since then. Uploads run in transactions of up to 150 records. A record whose cloud copy is newer, or soft-deleted, is refused and archived in syncConflicts ; the replaced version of an overwritten record is archived too. The Resolve sync conflicts dialog lets the organiser choose. Audit events are append-only and created in plain batches. Automatic per-action cloud writes exist in TournamentContext but are switched off ( AUTOMATIC_CLOUD_WRITES = false ). Details: docs/storage-and-scale.md and Backups, restore and cloud sync . 3. Live collaboration  For cloud tournaments on administrator devices, ballots , debates , teams and adjudicators are live : written to Firestore record by record as they change and received from other devices within seconds. Writes: saveLiveRecords → planLiveWrites ( application/liveSync.ts ) diffs what a command changed and writes field-level patches ( set with mergeFields ), one atomic writeBatch per command, bumping syncVersion . Listeners: createLiveSession ( application/liveSession.ts , adapter infrastructure/liveRepository.ts ) listens to whole teams and adjudicators collections and to debates and ballots of the active round only. Offline: the Firestore SDK's persistent cache (IndexedDB, src/lib/firebase.ts ) queues writes across reloads. Uploads and publishes wait up to 20 s for queued live writes to be acknowledged. Conflicts: incoming changes use the same baseline rule as a download; a locally edited record that the cloud also changed becomes a sync conflict. Two devices confirming different ballot versions of one debate is detected ( findConfirmationConflicts ) and shown, never resolved automatically. Live updates can be paused per device from the cloud status menu. Data-entry staff are not live. They read a redacted copy from /api/tournaments/{id}/assistant-data and send changes through /api/tournaments/{id}/data-entry-sync , which whitelists fields and checks permissions per record ( src/lib/dataEntrySync.ts ). Participants never touch the working copy. Private portals call /api/private/team (read) and /api/private/sync (queued ballots, feedback, check-ins; src/lib/privateSync.ts ). Debates in Firestore carry a cloud-only participantIds index so portals query only their own debates. Details: docs/live-collaboration.md . 4. Publishing the public site  The public site is a snapshot built at publish time , not a view of live data. After an upload or a release, the browser calls POST /api/tournaments/{id}/public-view ( application/publicView.ts ). The server reads the cloud collections and builds the public projection ( src/lib/publicView/projection.ts ): an allowlist of fields, filtered by release settings. Tabs with top-N limits and other aggregates are computed here ( derived.ts ). snapshot.ts splits it into sections: base sections ( tournament , rounds , teams , ...) and one round-{id} section per public round. Each is content-hashed and chunked (≤700 KB per document) under publicViews/{slug} . store.ts invalidates only the changed sections' cache tags ( revalidateTag ). Reads go through unstable_cache (Vercel Data Cache) with short CDN caching; a round fetched with its current hash is cached for a day. Public pages fetch /api/public/tournaments/{slug} (and /version to poll for a new publish). Public layouts render metadata server-side ( publicView/robots.ts , seo.ts ); the pages themselves are client components. Details: docs/public-pages-and-notifications.md , Public pages and releases . Server routes  All server routes live in src/app/api/** and use the Admin SDK from src/lib/firebaseAdmin.ts (credentials from FIREBASE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_JSON or application default credentials).
